name: Dirty bulk

lead: A dirty bulk means eating a large calorie surplus without closely tracking food quality or macros, often from calorie-dense foods such as burgers and fries. People use it to add size quickly, planning to cut the extra fat afterward.

Bodybuilding sources describe it as producing fast weight gain, including some muscle, along with substantial fat. On looksmaxxing forums it is contrasted with the clean bulk and is often discussed by steroid users or very thin people who struggle to gain; many users advise against it for appearance, citing facial bloating.

paras: It is combined with resistance training, with intake well above maintenance and little food tracking. Reference sources give typical surpluses of roughly 500 to 1,000 kcal a day. Early gains include water and glycogen, and a harder cut usually follows.

It typically adds significant fat, requiring a harsher cut afterward, and bodybuilding references mention possible long-term effects on cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity. No legal restrictions apply; no trials compare it with lean bulking for appearance.

web.title: Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season
Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy

angle.text: Users dirty bulk to gain size quickly without tracking food closely, accepting extra fat that is cut afterward. It is contrasted with clean bulking and often discussed by steroid users. Comparisons between the two come mostly from lifter experience.

lead: A dirty bulk is a bulking strategy in which a person eats a large calorie surplus without carefully tracking macronutrients or food quality, often relying on calorie-dense foods such as burgers and fries.[1] People use it to put on body weight and muscle quickly for a bigger physique, accepting extra body fat that they plan to remove in a later cutting phase. It is contrasted with a clean bulk, which uses a smaller surplus and more controlled food choices to limit fat gain.[1][2]

Bodybuilding references describe dirty bulking as capable of producing rapid weight and muscle gain, but usually with significant body fat that typically calls for a more aggressive cutting phase afterward.[1] One online encyclopedia summary gives typical surpluses of roughly 500 to 1,000 kcal per day for dirty bulking versus 250 to 500 for clean bulking, and also notes possible effects on blood lipids and insulin sensitivity, though that source has internal inconsistencies and some of its figures are weakly sourced.[2] Peer-reviewed reviews of off-season nutrition for natural bodybuilders recommend a more moderate approach, a surplus of roughly 10 to 20 percent above maintenance and a target gain of about 0.25 to 0.5 percent of body weight per week for novice and intermediate lifters, which is the lean-bulk end of the spectrum that dirty bulking is contrasted with.[3]

In looksmaxxing communities the term appears mainly in debates over whether to gain weight quickly or slowly, with many posters prioritising a lean, defined face and therefore recommending against it.[4][5] In strength-training forums, lifters describe dirty bulks as phases they entered for rapid scale gain, for hunger-driven recovery, or as a rest from strict tracking, and some later describe the fat gained and the cut that followed.[6][7][8][9]

paras: Bulking is a phase of eating in a net positive energy balance to support muscle growth, typically alternated with cutting.[1][2] Wikipedia's bodybuilding article explains that most competitors gain muscle in the off-season and then, roughly 12 to 14 weeks from competition, lose as much body fat as possible while preserving muscle.[1] The size of the surplus determines how much fat accompanies the gain: a larger surplus or longer bulk adds more body fat.[1]

In a dirty bulk the lifter prioritises total calories over food quality and does not tightly track macronutrients, a style Wikipedia describes as eating a large surplus without working out exact amounts, often with junk food.[1] Some lifters reportedly prefer it because it removes the pressure of strict meal planning.[1]

Grokipedia traces the roots of mass-building to nineteenth- and early twentieth-century strongman culture, noting Eugen Sandow's role in systematic training and the first major physique competition in 1901, the Weider brothers' promotion of mass-building through Your Physique (1940) and Joe Weider's 1954 Power and Bulk Routine, and the Golden Era (1970s to 1980s), when off-season mass-building before contest cutting became standard, with Arnold Schwarzenegger given as an example.[2] It adds that by the 1980s explicit calorie counting with about a 500 kcal daily excess was common.[2]

A clean bulk aims to add muscle with little fat gain through a modest surplus, sometimes using alternating higher- and lower-calorie days; it takes longer but is described as more precise.[1][2] Dirty bulking is described as faster on the scale but more fat-heavy, with one summary estimating a timeline of roughly 1.5 to 3 months for a 6 kg gain versus 4 to 8 months for clean bulking.[2]

Early scale gains from either approach include glycogen and water, so not all added weight is tissue.[2] Wikipedia gives approximate muscle-gain expectations for a novice lifting about seven hours per week of 4 to 7 kg per year, falling to roughly 2 to 7 kg per year after two years and less thereafter.[1] A T Nation member reflecting on a dirty bulk wrote that gaining a lot of fat after dropping weight may have made it look like muscle had been gained when it was fat and water.[10]

In general terms, a dirty bulk means eating well above maintenance calories on most days while training with progressive resistance exercise, without weighing portions or hitting set protein, carbohydrate and fat targets. Foods commonly named by lifters include burgers, pizza, fries, milkshakes and other calorie-dense meals, often alongside staples such as eggs, rice and milk.[1][5][11] Practitioners say the appeal is simplicity: no logging, easier social eating, and a steadily rising scale number, which Wikipedia notes some lifters find psychologically easier than strict meal planning.[1]

Dirty bulks are usually described as time-limited. Lifters talk about a phase of weeks to a few months followed by a cut, in which calories are reduced to lose the fat that came with the gain; bodybuilding references place the competition cut at about 12 to 14 weeks.[1][2] Lifters on T Nation describe entering a dirty bulk to make quick scale gains for a transformation challenge, or to get over strict tracking, and then dieting down afterwards.[8][9][12]

sections.h: Research on surplus size and weight gain
paras: A 2019 narrative review by Iraki and colleagues in the journal Sports examined nutrition for natural bodybuilders in the off-season. It recommended a hyper-energetic diet of about 10 to 20 percent above maintenance, a weekly weight gain of about 0.25 to 0.5 percent of body weight for novice and intermediate bodybuilders, with advanced lifters being more conservative, protein of 1.6 to 2.2 g per kg per day, moderate fat, and carbohydrate filling the remaining calories. The authors state the goal of the off-season as increasing muscle mass without adding unnecessary body fat.[3]

A 2019 review in Frontiers in Nutrition by Slater and colleagues asked whether an energy surplus is required to maximise hypertrophy from resistance training. It reports that the specific surplus required is unknown, that an energy surplus can have an anabolic effect independent of training, and that common textbook guidance, which is based on the energy content of the tissue gained, probably fails to account for other energetically costly processes and for individual factors such as training experience.[13]

Wikipedia's bodybuilding article gives approximate natural muscle-gain expectations of about 4 to 7 kg in the first year for a novice lifting around seven hours a week, 2 to 7 kg per year after two years and 1 to 5 kg per year after five.[1] Because those figures are much smaller than the pounds a dirty bulk can add to the scale, lifters and writers commonly point out that a share of any rapid gain is fat, along with glycogen and water.[1][2]

Clean bulking and lean bulking use a smaller, tracked surplus and more controlled food choices.[1][2] Bodybuilding sources also describe alternating higher- and lower-calorie days as a way to limit fat gain.[1] Recomposition, in which a lifter trains at around maintenance calories, is the slow end of the same spectrum. In looksmaxxing language, the choice often connects to facial leanness: many posters prefer slower gain so the face does not look puffy, while others, such as very thin posters, argue that eating more freely is what lets them gain at all.[4][5]

Wikipedia's bodybuilding article warns of possible long-term effects of dirty bulking on cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity.[1] A Grokipedia summary mentions raised cholesterol and triglycerides and insulin resistance risk from refined carbohydrates, and nutritional imbalances with disproportionate fat gain at large surpluses, but it flags that some of its citations do not clearly support its claims.[2]

No studies found. Research on bulking more broadly has compared moderate and large calorie surpluses over short periods; one encyclopedia summary reports similar muscle thickness gains over eight weeks at roughly 5 and 15 percent surpluses, with less fat gain at the lower one, though its sourcing is uneven.[2]

On looksmax.org, threads asking whether to clean or dirty bulk commonly draw replies favouring clean bulking, with some users saying dirty bulking is better suited to people using steroids.[4] Other threads show younger users asking the question while eating large amounts of sugar and processed food.[5]

On T Nation, one user describes a go-to calorie-dense meal during a 2016 dirty bulk; another says a bulk that was not completely dirty left them feeling they had put on muscle and had gotten over scale obsession; another writes that a dirty bulk until February produced a lot of fat and left them losing weight afterward.[11][12][8] Another poster extended a three-month bulk to 4.5 months with the last six weeks dirty for a transformation challenge, and another says a kettlebell-based dirty bulk took them from 73 to 77 kg while their legs grew.[9][7]

lore.intro: Forum users generally treat dirty bulking as the lower-effort alternative to clean bulking and mostly discourage it where facial leanness is the goal, while lifters on strength forums describe both its speed and its fat cost.[4][5][8]
